lawyer:
Azizur Rahman Chowdhury with Mohd Feroz and Md Abdul Mannan, Advocates — For the Appellant. 
Dewan AMS Zaman with Osman Gani, Advocates — For the Respondent.
parties:
Osmanullah being dead his legal heirs, Kasimullah & others ------ Plaintiff-Appellants
vs
Faizullah & others ------ Defendant-Respondent
full_judgment:
This Second Appeal at the instance of the plaintiff appellant is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30-4-1973 passed in Title Appeal No.122 of 1973 by Mr MA Wahab, Special Judge and ex-officio Additional District Judge, Sylhet reversing those dated 24-7-1972 passed in Title Suit No.166 of 1970 by he learned Munsif, 1st Court, Sylhet decreeing the suit on contest against defendant No.1 with cost and ex-parte against the rest without cost and declaring that the ex-parte order dated 14-11-1969 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 491/ 1969 under section 143A East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of the said Court for correction of the record of rights in respect of the suit-land is illegal, void., fraudulent and without jurisdiction. 

 3. The plaintiff later on by a petition got settlement of the suit-property up to 1376 BS from the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property and his petition for renewal of the lease was under consideration; that one Ahsanullah in the meantime filed a Miscellaneous Case No.413 of 1968 under section 143 A of the East Bangal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the plaintiff on his prayer was added as a party in the same under Order 1 rule 10 Code of Civil Procedure and then contested the Miscellaneous Case, but Ahsanullah later on withdrew the case and set up the principal defendant No.1 Faizullah to file another Miscellaneous Case No.419 of 1969 by fabricating some false documents and clandestinely secured an ex parte order on 14-11-69 for correction of the record of rights in his favour, though he has had no right title or possession in the said land; that no notice was served on the said Basanta Kumar Bhatta-charjee or his co-sharers. The plaintiff however came to know about the Miscellaneous Case No.491 of 1969 when defendant No.1 gave out in the locality towards the last part of March, 1970 that he had secured an order for correction of the record of rights in his favour in respect of the suit-land. Hence, the present suit against the defendant No. 1 and the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property, Sylhet as pro-forma defendant No.2. 

 10. Mr Azizur Rahman Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant has firstly submitted that the impugned judgment of the Court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal and as such the same should be set aside. To elaborate his argument, the learned Advocate has drawn my attention to the impugned judgment of the Court of appeal below as well as the judgment of the trial Court and then submitted that the trial Court as to the maintainability of the suit and bar of limitation held that the said issues were not pressed before him at the time of trial but still he came to a finding that by suppression of notices the impugned order in Miscellaneous Case No.491 of 1969 was passed on 14-11-69 and the instant suit was filed within time on 1-5-70. He also found that there was nothing to show against the maintainability of the suit; hence he answered the above two issues in favour of the plaintiff. But the lower Appellate Court heard the learned Advocate for the defendant-appellant on the point of maintainability of the suit and ultimately found that the plaintiff had no locus standi to institute the suit and the same was not also maintainable and hence allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned judgment and decree of the trial Court without making any finding as to the question of fraud as determined by the trial Court. It is further submitted by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the lower appellate Court did not at all reverse the findings of the trial Court on the question of fraud and also adverse possession, not to speak of adverting to the reasoning of the trial Court for coming to such findings. The learned Advocate for the appellant further submits that the plaintiff had subsisting interest and possession in the suit-land at the time of passing the order dated 14-11-1969 under section 143A East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act but he was not purposely made a party to the said proceeding. Of course, the original owner of the suit land Basanta Kumar Bhattacharjee and his co-sharer Ranadhir were made parties in that application for correction of the record of rights, but admittedly no notice was duly served upon them. The learned Advocate for the appellant therefore contends that the summons was suppressed by fraudulent means and the ex parte order was obtained surreptitiously. He however asserted that the plaintiff had locus-standi to file the present suit challenging the ex-parte order dated 14-11-1969 of the Miscellaneous Case, though he was not made a party in the same. He claimed his interest in the said property because of his caretaker ship of the interest of the said original owner Basanta Kumar Bhattacharjee, and further on his departure from this country to India, his property became enemy property and the plaintiff then took lease of the same from the Custodian of the Enemy Property by a regular document of lease dated 19-2-1970 and, as such, the plaintiff had every right to challenge the ex parte order passed in the Miscellaneous Case under section 143A of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by filing the present suit and the suit was therefore quite maintainable. 

 11. Mr Dewan AMS Zaman, the learned Advocate for the defendant-respondent, on the other hand, submits that the plaintiff had no locus-standi to institute the suit as he could not show his legal character under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act to be entitled to a declaration of his right, title and interest in the suit-land and a further declaration to the effect that the ex parte order dated 14-11-69 in Misc. Case under section 143A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was false, fraudulent and void ab-initio. The learned Advocate further argued that, it was of course the claim of the plaintiff that he was a lessee in the suit-land which was declared as Enemy Property and thus being a lessee in possession of the suit-land, he was competent to challenge the ex parte order of correction of the record of right in the suit-land by institution of the suit, but a lessee was not a necessary party in a suit like this wherein the lessor was already made a party. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate referred to a decision in the case of Saifuddin Ahmed vs Deputy Custodian, Enemy Property Management Board, reported in 31 DLR 107. He further contended that the suit could be maintainable, had there been a prayer for declaration of plaintiff''s right, title or interest in the suit land together with a prayer for consequential relief. It is further submitted that a suit for a mere declaration to the effect that the impugned ex parte order was false, fraudulent, void, ab-initio and not binding on the plaintiff was not maintainable. Hence that learned Special Judge and ex-officio District Judge rightly held that the plaintiff had no locus standi to institute the suit and the same was not maintainable. 

 12. The learned Advocate for the respondents, of course submitted that there was no finding by the lower appellate Court as to the question of alleged fraud committed in obtaining the ex parte order in the proceedings under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as found by the trial Court, but his contention was that this would not affect the merit of the decision of the lower appellate Court allowing the appeal and dismissing the suit on the ground of maintainability. As to the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant that the minimum requirements for passing the ex parte order dated 14-11-69 in the proceeding under section 143A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act were not complied with, apart from the fraudulent suppression of the process or notice and non-compliance of the provisions of inquiry as required under sub-section (4) of section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by local Revenue Officer in respect of possession of the parties over the land in question before passing such order. It is not clear whether the inquiry as required under the law was properly held in this case. The original records of the Miscellaneous Case are not available before this Court to verify the above contention regarding service of notices and the compliance of the provision of sub-section 4 of section 143A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 14. The learned Advocate for the appellant has however taken me through the entire provisions of section 143A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and tried to show the procedure to be followed in the case of disposal of an application under section 143A of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The said section 143A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act reads as follows: 

 Sub-section (13) of the East Pakistan State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides that: 

 18. Now, it may be pointed out that section 143A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is a special provision inserted in East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in 1965, of course the same has been repealed by another Ordinance No. LXIV of 1975. Its purposes was for correcting mistake in the record of rights on the basis of possession of the parties in the case land. However, the scope of section 143A has been discussed in a decision in the case of Assistant Custodiaiv Enemy Property (L&B) Tangail vs Bholanath Guha and ors reported in 36 DLR (AD) 79 and their Lordships have observed in the following terms therein, 

 "An application under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not a suit for declaration of title but is a proceeding for rectification of mistakes in the record of right prepared on the basis of possession in the land in question. The scheme of the section shows the possession is the material question. This was a special provision and this section was inserted after section 143 by East Pakistan. Ordinance VIII of 1965. It was however omitted after a few years by Ordinance LXIV of 1975". 

 "It is well settled that material consideration in a case under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is a question of possession. Whatever may be the defect in title, if it is found that the appellants have been possessing the case land when the record of right was prepared, they are entitled to have their names recorded." 

 19. The learned Advocate for the defendant-respondent, on the other hand, submits that the alleged lease was given in the year 1970 according to the showing of the plaintiff and it is the contention on behalf of the defendant that the property was not declared Enemy Property and there was no valid lease granted in favour of the plaintiff. At this stage it may be noticed that the ex parte order which is under challenge in the suit was passed on 14-11-1969 by the learned Munsif in consideration of an application under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and granting of the alleged lease to the plaintiff by the enemy authority is subsequent to the passing of the said order. Hence, in my view subsequent lease is not material for consideration of the question as to whether the plaintiff had subsisting interest and possession in the land in question at the time of passing the ex parte order in the Miscellaneous Case under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Therefore, in my view, both the Courts unnecessarily went into the discussion as to the alleged granting of lease of the property as enemy property to the plaintiff while determining the question of locus-standi of the plaintiff to challenge the order dated 14-11-69 passed in the Miscellaneous Case. Admittedly the plaintiff was not made a party in the Miscellaneous Case under section 143A of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Now the question is whether he can challenge the ex parte order passed in the above proceeding under section 143A East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by institution of this present suit. It is contended by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit-land at the relevant time as a caretaker of the said Basanta Kumar Bhattacharjee and, as such, he ought to have been made a party in the said proceedings along with said Basanta Kumar and that having not been done, he was seriously prejudiced, particularly when there was suppression of process upon the said Basanta Kumar and another. Hence, in view of the above submissions on the scope of section 143A, the question of possession was very material in determining the locus-standi of the plaintiff for institution of the suit, but unfortunately, both the Courts below over-looked this aspect of the matter and failed to come to any specific finding as to the possession of the parties over the suit-land at the relevant time. It further appears from the impugned judgment of the lower appellate Court that he found the suit to be not maintainable mainly on the ground that the suit was not instituted for declaration of title and for any other consequential relief. It is true that, if the plaintiff wants to base his claim on the basis of his alleged lease from the Enemy Property authority which was admittedly a subsequent event, then possibly that would not help him. 

 20. However for maintainability of the suit as contended there ought to have been a prayer for declaration of right, title and other consequential relief and for that purpose, the plaintiff could be given an option by the lower appellate Court to amend the plaint and incorporate such prayer for the purpose of the maintainability of the suit. Now, in the instant case, it appears that the plaintiff has come with his claims of interest and possession in the suit land at the relevant time on the basis of his caretaker ship of the suit-land, on behalf of the actual owner of the said land i.e. Basanta Kumar Bhattacharjee and to maintain the suit on that basis as I have said earlier that the determination of the question of possession of the parties over the land at the relevant time was very much material but evidence on the question of possession from both the sides appears to be very meagre and insufficient and further the record of the suit does not show as to whether there was an inquiry by the local revenue officer under sub-section 4(b) of the section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act with regard to the possession of the parties at the relevant time and that could be correctly ascertained only by calling for the records of the Miscellaneous case under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and in this respect both the Courts failed to apply their judicial mind and to determine the question of actual possession of the parties in the suit-land at the relevant time. The learned Advocate for the defendant-respondent however raised some question with regard to the lease deed Exhibit 1 which shows that it was granted for one year that is for 1373 BS. But the receipt shows the granting of lease for the period of 4 years at a time which is not permissible in law. Of course, it appears that after 1376, the plaintiff filed an application for renewal of the said lease but nothing available on the record whether such renewal was at all granted. 

 24. Mr Zaman, the learned Advocate for the respondent also argued that as against the order passed in the Miscellaneous case under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, there is provision for appeal before the learned District judge, the plaintiff could have sought relief to that very Court after passing of the ex parte order, if the relief was not otherwise barred by any other provisions of law, but the same having not been done the plaintiff wrongly instituted the suit for setting aside the impugned ex parte order passed by the learned Munsif. I do not find any substance in this contention of the learned Advocate, as the plaintiff was not made a party in the proceeding under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and secondly, fraud has been alleged in the plaint against the contesting defendant in obtaining the said ex parte order. It is well settled that an ex parte order under the general law can be set aside by taking resort to the provision of Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure also by review or by way of instituting a suit on the ground of fraud. 

 25. Therefore, in this respect, I think there is no bar in the institution of the suit on the ground of fraud without availing of the provision for appeal under the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The plaintiff is however required to establish his locus-standi and the maintainability of the suit. Having considered all aspects of the matter and the relevant provisions of law and the decisions cited above by the parties before me, I am of the view that the lower appellate Court committed gross illegality in determining the question of locus-standi of the plaintiff and maintainability of the suit without coming to a positive finding as to possession of the parties over the suit-land at the relevant time i.e. in 1969 when the application under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was filed in the Court of the learned Munsif for correction of record-of-rights and thereafter when the suit was instituted. At the same time, it is not at all proper for the lower appellate Court to avoid coming to a finding as to the question of fraud on discussion of the materials on record although the trial Court came to such a finding in clear terms. Therefore, the judgment of the Court of appeal below is not at all a proper judgment of reversal and the same is liable to be set aside. 

 In the result, this appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below are set aside and the appeal is sent back on remand to the Court of the learned Additional District Judge and Special Judge for re-hearing and determining the material points as have been pointed out, on the basis of the materials on record and, if necessary, to take further additional evidence from both the sides and particularly with regard to the inquiry report of the revenue officer, if any, of the local. Circle Office, Revenue, concerned and compliance of the provisions of sub-section 4 of section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and for that purpose, if necessary, the records of that Miscellaneous Case under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act may be called for and on consideration thereof to dispose of the appeal by a proper judgment in accordance with law in light of the observations made above. In the facts and circumstances of the case, there will be no order as to costs in this second appeal. The learned Advocate for the appellants is permitted to take back his application for additional grounds in view of the above decision.
